title: MYP Year 1 Slide Decks Built for Thinking, Practice, and Reflection
summary: A practical look at the MYP Year 1 mathematics slide decks and how their lesson flow supports inquiry, problem-solving, and reflection.
author: Guy Haik
body:
# MYP Year 1 Slide Decks Built for Thinking, Practice, and Reflection

Good teaching materials do more than place information on a screen. They create a rhythm for the lesson: orient students, give them something to think about, make space to try, and then pause to reflect on what they have learned.

The **MYP Year 1 mathematics slide decks** are designed around that rhythm. They provide a coherent sequence for the year while leaving room for students to explain, question, make connections, and solve problems in their own ways.

![Students working together in a classroom](myp-year-1-classroom.jpg)

*Classroom image from [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/children-sitting-on-chair-inside-room-during-daytime-photo-1509062522246-3755977927d7).* 

## Start with the curriculum map

The best place to understand the structure of the materials is the [IB MYP Mathematics Curriculum Map](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1QnWSTHUj95ZkpCW7dzpeFoO-WnHiJ9pF8EldCU9y61E/edit?usp=drivesdk). It shows how the units and topics fit together across the year, so individual decks can be used as part of a planned progression rather than as isolated lessons.

The [MYP Year 1 slide-deck repository](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kY1PdkwcjteoQrAX-sw6CcqWm9sAg0qF?usp=drive_link) contains the decks organized by unit. The sequence begins with number systems and operations, then develops through algebraic thinking, ratio and proportion, geometry and measurement, data and probability, and coordinates and transformations.

## A clear lesson arc

Each deck is organized to help a teacher move from intention to understanding. A typical sequence includes:

1. **Learning objectives** that make the destination visible to students.
2. **MYP framing** that connects the lesson to key and related concepts, as well as relevant assessment criteria.
3. **Explanations and worked examples** that model the mathematical idea without making the lesson purely lecture-based.
4. **Guided practice and problems** that let students apply the idea while the teacher can notice misconceptions.
5. **Inquiry prompts and challenges** that ask students to justify, compare, generalize, or find more than one way to represent an idea.
6. **An exit ticket** that provides a concise check of understanding and a moment of reflection before the lesson ends.

This structure makes the decks useful as both a teaching guide and a student-facing learning path. The slides are not just a sequence of answers; they are prompts for mathematical activity.

## Inquiry activities that ask students to make meaning

Inquiry appears in the decks through questions that go beyond “calculate.” Students may be asked to create different descriptions of a number, decide which representation is most useful in a context, explain why a method works, or investigate what changes and what stays constant.

These prompts support the MYP emphasis on communication and reasoning. They give students a reason to talk about mathematics, not only perform it, and they create natural openings for pair work, class discussion, and written justification.

## Problems with purpose

The problem sets are varied enough to support progression. Some questions build fluency with a new skill; others require students to apply it in an unfamiliar situation or explain their reasoning. Worked examples establish a model, while later tasks ask students to take more responsibility for choosing a method and communicating a conclusion.

Because the problems are embedded in the lesson flow, teachers can use them flexibly: as guided examples, individual practice, discussion starters, extension tasks, or quick formative checks.

## Real-world scenarios that give mathematics a reason

The decks also place mathematical ideas in recognizable settings. Examples include representing local or global statistics, comparing quantities, working with areas and measurements, and making decisions about which form of information is most useful.

These contexts are not decoration. They help students see why a representation, operation, or model might matter. A number can be more than an answer on a page: it can describe a population, a distance, a space, a change, or a decision.

## Exit tickets that close the loop

The exit tickets offer a short end-of-lesson checkpoint. They often combine a few focused questions with a reflection prompt, allowing students to show what they can do and articulate what they understand.

For teachers, this creates useful evidence for the next lesson. The responses can reveal whether students need another representation, more practice with a particular procedure, or a deeper challenge. For students, the final pause reinforces that reflection is part of learning—not an optional extra after the “real” mathematics is finished.

## A resource that supports—not replaces—teaching

The decks are designed to give lessons a dependable structure while leaving the teacher room to respond to the students in front of them. A teacher can slow down at a misconception, extend an inquiry, change the grouping, or use a problem as the starting point for discussion.

That balance is the value of a strong slide deck: it reduces preparation friction without turning teaching into pressing “next.” The curriculum map provides the year-long architecture; the individual decks provide the lesson-level pathway; and the inquiry, problems, real-world scenarios, and exit tickets keep students doing the thinking.

[Browse the MYP Year 1 slide decks](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kY1PdkwcjteoQrAX-sw6CcqWm9sAg0qF?usp=drive_link) or [open the curriculum map](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1QnWSTHUj95ZkpCW7dzpeFoO-WnHiJ9pF8EldCU9y61E/edit?usp=drivesdk) to see how the pieces fit together.

title: Why Are We Always Waiting to Start Living?
summary: What we lose when “later” becomes the only time we allow ourselves to enjoy life.
author: Guy Haik
body:
# Why Are We Always Waiting to Start Living?

There is a quote often attributed to the Dalai Lama that describes a strange contradiction: we sacrifice our health to make money, then sacrifice our money trying to recover our health. We worry so much about the future that we forget to enjoy the present—and eventually, life passes us by.

Whether or not the Dalai Lama actually said those words, the idea behind them is worth considering. How often do we tell ourselves:

- “I’ll enjoy life when I have more money.”
- “I’ll relax when I finish this project.”
- “I’ll travel when I can afford it.”
- “I’ll spend more time with my family when work becomes less demanding.”

There is always a “when.” Sometimes that “when” never arrives.

## Why are we so focused on the future?

Planning for tomorrow is not a bad thing. We need to save money, build careers, care for our health, and prepare for unexpected problems. The problem begins when preparing for the future consumes the present.

We can become so focused on creating a better life later that we do not notice we are already living our life now. A person might spend twenty years working toward financial security, only to discover that they missed many of the experiences they were working so hard to afford.

We are constantly told to invest in our future. But what happens when the future becomes the only place where we allow ourselves to be happy?

## The cost of always saying “later”

Think about the things you have postponed. Maybe there is somewhere you want to travel, a hobby you want to pursue, someone you want to spend more time with, or something you have always wanted to learn. Maybe you simply want to slow down.

Sometimes the reason is completely practical: you genuinely do not have the time or money. But sometimes the answer is just “later.” Later is an easy word to use when we are afraid to make a change, and it can become a habit.

We keep postponing what makes life meaningful because we are waiting for perfect circumstances. But life rarely gives us perfect circumstances.

## Are you living or just preparing to live?

There is nothing wrong with ambition, financial security, or building a career. These things are supposed to support our lives, not replace them.

Sometimes we treat the present as a waiting room for the future: waiting for the weekend, vacation, retirement, the right relationship, more money, better health, greater success, or more confidence. But the present is not an obstacle standing between us and the life we want. It is the only part of life we actually experience.

The future matters, but the future is always becoming the present. If we spend our entire lives waiting for tomorrow, tomorrow eventually becomes today—and we may simply continue waiting.

## What does a balanced life look like?

The answer is not to stop thinking about the future. A healthy life probably requires both preparation and presence:

- Save money, but allow yourself to enjoy some of what you earn.
- Work hard, but remember why you are working.
- Care for your health, but do not become so focused on optimization that you forget to enjoy being alive.
- Plan your future, but do not make the future responsible for your happiness.

If you feel like you are constantly working, worrying, and waiting for life to begin, try asking yourself:

- What am I constantly postponing?
- What am I working so hard for?
- If my financial situation improved tomorrow, what would I do differently?
- Who would I spend more time with?
- What experiences do I want to have?
- What makes me feel genuinely alive?
- If nothing about my current lifestyle changed for ten years, would I be happy with where it takes me?

You do not necessarily need to change your entire life after answering these questions. Sometimes one small change is enough: call someone you have not spoken to in a long time, start the hobby you have been postponing, spend an evening without your phone, take a walk without having somewhere to be, or have a real conversation.

## Don’t wait for permission to live

There will always be another bill, responsibility, goal, or problem to solve. If we wait until everything is under control before allowing ourselves to enjoy life, we may spend our entire lives waiting.

The future deserves our preparation, but the present deserves our attention. Maybe the goal is to build a future that does not require us to sacrifice the present.

Eventually, all of us will reach the end of our lives. The question is not whether we will get there. The question is what we will have done along the way.

title: How to Deal With an Angry Person Without Making Things Worse
summary: Emotional intelligence can change the direction of a difficult conversation without excusing harmful behavior.
author: Guy Haik
body:
# How to Deal With an Angry Person Without Making Things Worse

When someone is angry, our first instinct is often to fight back, defend ourselves, or prove our point. But responding to anger with more anger can quickly turn a difficult moment into a competition over who can shout louder.

If the situation is unsafe or someone is becoming violent, create distance and get appropriate help. Emotional intelligence never requires you to tolerate abuse or threatening behavior. When it is safe to engage, however, there are ways to change the emotional direction of the interaction.

## Anger may be covering something else

Anger is sometimes the most visible part of a more complicated experience. A person may feel disrespected, embarrassed, rejected, frightened, powerless, or simply unheard. Understanding this does not mean agreeing with their behavior. It means trying to see the person behind the behavior.

Daniel Goleman’s *Emotional Intelligence* tells a memorable story about Terry Dobson, an aikido student who encountered a violent drunk man on a train in Japan. Before Dobson could intervene, an elderly passenger spoke to the man warmly about sake, his wife, and his garden. The man gradually relaxed and began sharing the grief beneath his aggression: he had lost his wife, home, and job.

The elderly man did not defeat him. He changed the emotional direction of the encounter. The story is not a magic formula, but it illustrates several useful principles.

## Four ways to respond

1. **Do not automatically match the other person’s intensity.** If someone raises their voice and you immediately raise yours, the temperature usually increases. Staying calm does not guarantee that they will calm down, but it prevents you from adding more fuel.
2. **Listen before trying to solve the problem.** Listening does not mean agreeing. It gives you a chance to understand what the person is actually upset about—and can help them feel heard before they try to hear you.
3. **Look beneath the anger.** Ask yourself what the person could be experiencing right now. The current argument may be connected to fear, shame, frustration, or something that happened earlier.
4. **Change the direction of the conversation.** A genuine question, a moment of empathy, or a pause can interrupt an argument that is going nowhere. The aim is to create an opportunity for a more thoughtful conversation, not to manipulate the other person.

## Boundaries still matter

This is especially important with children. A child may shout because they are frustrated, refuse to participate because they are afraid of failing, or become aggressive because they feel embarrassed. Adults can acknowledge the feeling while setting a clear boundary: “I understand that you’re angry. But you cannot hit anyone. Let’s talk about what happened when you’re ready.”

The same principle applies to adults. Emotional intelligence is not passive endurance. You can acknowledge someone’s feelings without agreeing with their conclusions. You can be firm without being cruel, and you can end a conversation when it is no longer productive:

> We’re both too upset to have a productive conversation right now. Let’s talk later.

You do not have to win every argument or remain in an unsafe situation to prove that you are understanding.

## A question worth asking

Before reacting, pause and ask: **What is happening here?** What are they feeling? What am I feeling? What is actually causing the conflict? Is this the right time to solve it? Would listening—or giving the conversation some space—help?

Emotional intelligence is not perfect control. It is the skill of recognizing emotions, including your own, and making a deliberate choice about how to respond. Sometimes the strongest response to anger is enough calm and curiosity to see the human being underneath it.

title: How to Practice Guitar So You Actually Make Progress
summary: A simple, sustainable approach to practice that turns limited time into noticeable progress.
author: Guy Haik
body:
# How to Practice Guitar So You Actually Make Progress

You do not need hours of free time to improve at guitar. You need a clear goal, a manageable plan, and feedback that helps you spend your practice time on the right things.

## Start with the music you want to make

Practice becomes easier to sustain when it connects to a song, sound, or skill you genuinely care about. We can use that motivation as the starting point, then build the technique around it: chord changes, rhythm, picking, ear training, or whatever will help you play more confidently.

## Choose one small target

Instead of trying to “get better at guitar,” choose a result you can hear. Play the verse without stopping. Change between two chords cleanly. Keep a steady beat for one minute. Small targets make progress visible and give each session a purpose.

## Make the hard part easier to repeat

When something feels stuck, slow it down and isolate it. Short, accurate repetitions teach your hands more effectively than rushing through an entire song and repeating the same mistake. A good lesson gives you a practical way to break a challenge into steps you can repeat at home.

## Build a routine you can keep

A consistent 15–20 minutes can be more valuable than an occasional marathon session. Your practice plan should fit your schedule and energy, not compete with them. The aim is a routine that feels achievable enough to return to—and structured enough to create momentum.

Guy's one-on-one lessons are tailored to each student's capabilities, goals, and needs. If you want a clear next step and an encouraging plan for making music, [book a lesson](../booking.html).

title: What to Expect From a Private Guitar Lesson
summary: How personalized guitar coaching builds confidence, technique, and a path forward.
author: Guy Haik
body:
# What to Expect From a Private Guitar Lesson

A first lesson should feel useful, welcoming, and connected to what you want to play. You do not need to arrive with perfect technique—or even a clearly defined goal. We start from where you are and shape the lesson around where you want to go.

## A plan built around you

Every student brings a different background, learning style, and reason for picking up the guitar. Some people want to play favorite songs. Others want stronger fundamentals, better rhythm, or the confidence to perform. Guy adapts the instruction to your current capabilities and goals rather than asking you to fit a fixed program.

## Practical progress from the first session

You will work on something you can take away and practice: a chord progression, a rhythm pattern, a riff, or a technique that unlocks the next step. Clear explanations and focused exercises make it easier to know what to do between lessons and why it matters.

## Confidence is part of the lesson

Learning an instrument can be frustrating when every mistake feels like evidence that you are not improving. A supportive, student-centered approach changes that experience. We slow down when needed, notice what is working, and turn challenges into manageable repetitions so your confidence grows alongside your playing.

Guy has delivered private guitar instruction since 2023 and has built long-term client relationships through tailored one-on-one coaching. Ready to get started? [Book your first lesson](../booking.html) and choose a time that works for you.
